title: The living soil
teaches: Soil organisms, the underground food chain, and how plant roots feed the microbes around them

blocks.text: Lesson 1 described soil as broken rock mixed with a little organic matter, which is an accurate description of a pot of sterilised compost. A handful of soil from a garden bed is very different because it is packed with living things.

blocks.caption: Typical numbers of organisms in a teaspoon of healthy garden soil

blocks.text: A single teaspoon of healthy garden soil holds between a hundred million and a billion [[bacteria|clay]], several thousand to tens of thousands of [[protozoa|water]], a few dozen [[nematodes|silt]], and one to tens of metres of fungal strands that are individually too fine to see.[^census] Alongside them live mites, springtails, beetle larvae and, in a full spadeful, several earthworms. Biologists have yet to formally name most of these species.[^unnamed]
Every organism in that soil is trying to make a living, usually by eating something else. Tracing their meals reveals a food web anchored by plants, built around a lively underground trade.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Healthy soil is crowded: a teaspoon holds hundreds of millions of bacteria and metres of fungal thread.
Most soil creatures survive on other soil life, dead plants, or the sugars released by living roots.

blocks.text: The food web begins at the roots. A plant makes sugar in its leaves using sunlight, then pumps up to a fifth of that sugar out through its roots into the surrounding soil.[^rhizosphere] Rather than going to waste, these sugars pay the billions of bacteria and fungi that gather around the root.

blocks.caption: The soil food web: arrows point from the food to the organism that eats it
blocks.task: Tap a member and take it out to see what else disappears

blocks.text: As those bacteria grow, they absorb nitrogen and other nutrients from the soil. Next, larger microbes called protozoa and nematodes eat the bacteria. Because a bacterium contains a higher concentration of nitrogen than its predator needs, the predator excretes the excess as ammonium right next to the root.[^loop] The plant feeds the bacteria, the predators eat the bacteria, and the plant absorbs the leftover ammonium.

Fungi run their own trade network. Many fungal species grow directly into plant roots and extend long, fine threads far out into the soil, reaching into smaller pores than root hairs ever could. They trade the water and phosphorus they collect out there for the plant's sugar.[^mycorrhiza] Most garden vegetables join this partnership, though the cabbage family, spinach and beets go without. Because garden soil almost always contains these fungi already, buying packets of them rarely improves a bed. Keeping living roots in the ground and digging less will look after the fungi you already have.

Larger creatures handle the heavy lifting. Mites, springtails and woodlice chew fallen leaves into tiny fragments that bacteria and fungi can easily break down. Earthworms pull whole leaves underground and swallow soil as they burrow, leaving behind nutrient-rich casts and open channels that help water and roots move deeper.[^darwin]

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Plants release sugars from their roots to feed soil microbes.
Predators that eat bacteria release nitrogen by the roots, while fungi trade water and phosphorus for sugar.
Earthworms and chewing insects shred dead leaves, mix the soil, and open up channels.

blocks.text: The entire soil food web ultimately runs on two fuel sources: sugars from living roots, and dead plant matter. You can feed your soil by keeping plants growing in the bed for as much of the year as possible, and by topping it with dead plant material like compost and mulch, which we will cover in the next lesson.

On the other hand, a few common habits can starve or damage the web. Bare soil without living roots or mulch offers almost nothing to eat. Digging snaps fungal threads and floods the soil with air, causing bacteria to multiply rapidly and burn through organic matter.[^tillage] Waterlogged soil suffocates air-breathing organisms, while walking on a bed crushes the tiny spaces where soil life lives. When left undisturbed, this underground web binds the soil into the crumbly structure covered in Lesson 5.

blocks.caption: White fungal threads under old mulch show the food web breaking down dead wood

blocks.title: Try it in the garden
points: In spring or autumn, when the soil is moist, dig out one spadeful about 20 cm wide and 20 cm deep. Break it apart on a sack and count the earthworms. Ten or more indicates a well-fed soil, while fewer than five suggests the web is short on food.
Lift a patch of mulch or an old board that has rested on the soil for a few weeks, and look underneath for white fungal threads, springtails and woodlice. Write down what you find.

items.question: Roughly how many bacteria live in a teaspoon of healthy soil?
options: Hundreds of millions
About a hundred
A few thousand
None: soil is mineral
items.why: A teaspoon holds between a hundred million and a billion bacteria, depending on the soil. Fungi grow as long strands, so they are measured in metres of thread instead.

items.question: Why does a plant release sugar through its roots?
options: It feeds the microbes that help it get nutrients and water
It is leaking sap by accident
To poison pests in the soil
items.why: Root sugars feed bacteria and fungi. Protozoa eat those bacteria and release nitrogen, while partner fungi trade water and phosphorus for the sugar.

items.question: When a protozoan eats a bacterium, what happens to the bacterium's excess nitrogen?
options: It is released as ammonium, which plants can absorb
It escapes into the air as a gas
It stays locked inside the protozoan until it dies
items.why: Bacteria have a higher concentration of nitrogen than protozoa need, so the protozoan excretes the surplus right by the root.

items.question: What are these white threads growing under old mulch?
options: Fungi breaking down the mulch and feeding the soil
A disease that will attack living plants
Fine roots from a weed
items.why: Fine white strands on damp, decaying wood or leaves are fungi decomposing dead matter into soil nutrients.

items.question: How do earthworms help a garden bed?
options: They pull dead leaves down, mix the soil, and open burrows
They eat living plant roots
They make the soil much more acidic
items.why: Worms drag surface litter into the soil, leave nutrient-rich casts, and dig burrows that let water and roots travel downward.

items.question: Which practice does the most harm to the soil food web?
options: Digging a bed and leaving it bare all winter
Covering the soil with dead leaves
Growing a winter cover crop
items.why: Digging breaks up fungal networks, and bare soil has no living roots or surface litter to feed the web. Mulch and cover crops keep soil life fed.

items.question: If a spadeful of your garden bed only has two worms in it, what does that tell you?
options: The soil life is short of food or shelter
The soil is in ideal condition
There is too much compost in the bed
items.why: Finding fewer than five worms in a moist spadeful usually means there is little for them to eat, often because the soil is left bare, dug frequently, or low in organic matter.

learned: A teaspoon of healthy soil holds hundreds of millions of bacteria and metres of fungal thread.
Plants feed soil microbes with root sugars and receive nutrients and water in return.
Protozoa and nematodes release nitrogen when they eat bacteria, while fungi trade phosphorus and water for sugar.
Living roots and dead plants feed the web, whereas bare soil, digging, waterlogging and compaction damage it.

census.title: Counting soil life
census.text: These ranges come from the US Natural Resources Conservation Service's *Soil Biology Primer* for farmland and garden soils. Forest soils hold far more fungi—sometimes hundreds of metres of thread in a teaspoon—along with more nematodes. Counting soil bacteria is tricky because older lab methods only counted species that would grow in a petri dish, whereas modern DNA sequencing reveals many more.

unnamed.title: More microbes than people?
unnamed.text: Gardeners often repeat the claim that a teaspoon of soil holds more microbes than there are people on Earth (around eight billion). For a typical garden bed, that is a slight exaggeration, since a billion bacteria is one for every eight people. However, rich soils measured with DNA methods can reach ten billion cells per gram. Either way, a 2023 study led by Mark Anthony estimated that nearly 60% of all species on Earth live in the soil, and the vast majority have never been named.

rhizosphere.title: Rhizosphere and root exudates
rhizosphere.text: The thin zone of soil clinging to a root, just a few millimetres wide, is called the **rhizosphere**. The sugars, amino acids and organic acids that roots release into this zone are **root exudates**. Because of this constant food supply, microbes in the rhizosphere can be ten to a hundred times more crowded than in the rest of the soil.

loop.title: The microbial loop
loop.text: A bacterium's body contains roughly one part nitrogen for every five parts carbon. A protozoan needs less nitrogen—about one part nitrogen for every ten parts carbon—and it also burns off roughly half the carbon it eats for energy. As a result, a protozoan eating bacteria takes in far more nitrogen than its body can use, and excretes the rest as ammonium (NH₄⁺). Soil ecologists call this process the **microbial loop**.

mycorrhiza.title: Mycorrhizae
mycorrhiza.text: A fungus that forms a partnership with a plant root is **mycorrhizal**, from the Greek words for fungus and root. Most vegetables partner with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, which push branching structures inside root cells to trade nutrients. The individual fungal threads, called **hyphae**, are about a tenth the width of a root hair. Plants in the cabbage family (brassicas) and the beet family (including spinach and chard) do not form this partnership. Frequent digging and heavy doses of phosphorus fertilizer weaken mycorrhizal networks, since a plant flooded with free phosphorus stops feeding the fungus.

darwin.title: Darwin's last book
darwin.text: Charles Darwin's final book, published in 1881, was *The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms*. He spent decades studying earthworms: weighing their casts, measuring how fast stones sank into his fields as worms burrowed underneath them, and testing whether worms could hear his son play the bassoon (they couldn't, though they felt vibrations when the pot sat on a piano). He calculated that worms bring roughly ten to eighteen tonnes of soil per acre to the surface each year. When it came out, the book initially sold faster than *On the Origin of Species*.

tillage.title: Why digging burns organic matter
tillage.text: Turning soil with a spade or rototiller breaks apart soil clumps, exposing trapped organic matter to oxygen and hungry bacteria. The bacterial population spikes and rapidly consumes the carbon, releasing it into the air as carbon dioxide (CO₂). At the same time, digging shreds the long, delicate networks of fungal hyphae, which take months to regrow.
